name: Macrina the Younger

seo.title: St Macrina the Younger: the sister who taught Basil and Gregory
seo.description: Who Macrina the Younger was, in plain words: the sister who turned Basil round, her healings, her last prayer, her feast days and her words.

person.deathPlace: Annesi, on the river Iris, Pontus

band.lede: The eldest sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, whom Gregory called the Teacher.

picture.alt: A white stone statue of a young woman in a flowing cloak against a deep blue sky; she looks upward, one hand on her breast and a book held in the other.
picture.credit: Saint Macrina, statue on the colonnade of St Peter's Square, 1668, sculptor unknown. Photo by Alf van Beem, CC0.
picture.creator: Alf van Beem

card.line: The eldest sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, whom Gregory called the Teacher.

who: Macrina was the eldest sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. When her fiancé died, she never married. She turned Basil from his pride. She turned her family's household into a community of women who lived as equals. Gregory called her the Teacher. She wrote nothing, so almost everything we know comes from him.

roles.name: Abbess
roles.line: Of a community on the Iris

lines: Her father chose the young man

numbers.src: Life of Macrina, Gregory resolves to visit his sister

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 330, probably at Neocaesarea in Pontus, today **Niksar in Turkey**. No ancient source gives the year.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: On the family's estates. Her mother taught her from the Bible, not the poets. She knew every part of the Psalms.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **In 379 or 380**, of a fever, at her community on the river Iris in Pontus. Her brother Gregory was with her.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: Beside her mother, in the family grave at the church of the Holy Martyrs, about a mile away.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Thecla**, a secret name from a dream before her birth. **The Teacher**, in Gregory's dialogue. **Venerable Macrina**, in Orthodox churches. **Macrina of Caesarea**, in the Episcopal Church. **The Younger**, to tell her from her grandmother.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics and Orthodox. The Church of England and the Episcopal Church keep her day, and the ELCA remembers her.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In an 11th-century fresco in Kyiv, a veiled nun with both hands raised, palms out. On the colonnade of St Peter's Square, a young woman looking up, with a hand on her breast and a book in the other.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Nothing that survives. All we know of her comes through her brother Gregory.

portrait.alt: A fresco of Macrina standing in a grey-green veil and cloak over a white robe, a gold halo behind her head, both hands raised with the palms facing out.
portrait.credit: Saint Macrina the Younger, fresco, St Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv, 11th century. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A fresco in St Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv, from the 11th century. She stands veiled, with both hands raised. Public domain.

west.text: **ELCA**, with Basil and the two Gregorys.
**Catholic**, in the 1916 Roman Martyrology. She is not on the General Roman Calendar. Also the **Church of England**, with her brother Gregory of Nyssa, and the **Episcopal Church**.

east.text: **Greek** churches and the **OCA**. Also the **Russian Church**, on the old calendar. That is 1 August on today's calendar.

feasts.note: Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so 19 July falls on 1 August. Her grandmother, Macrina the Elder, has her own day in the Roman Martyrology, 14 January.

traits.title: steady in a disaster
traits.text: Her favourite brother, Naucratius, died suddenly, and their mother collapsed at the news. Macrina did not. She held her mother up, and “by her own steadfastness and imperturbability taught her mother's soul to be brave”.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the one support of her mother

traits.title: blunt with her brothers
traits.text: Basil came home from his studies “puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory”, and she took him in hand. Years later Gregory poured out his troubles at her deathbed. She told him to stop and count his blessings.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Basil's return and Gregory's last visit

traits.title: kept nothing
traits.text: She kept none of her share of the family property. It all went “into the priest's hands according to the divine command”. She never turned anyone away, and she never asked anyone for help.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory's last visit

traits.title: no ranks at home
traits.text: She talked her rich mother into living as an equal with her own maids. They shared “the same food, the same kind of bed”.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, mother and daughter

traits.title: a mother to the abandoned
traits.text: In a famine she picked up children abandoned by the roadside, and nursed and raised them herself. When she died, they wept the hardest. They called her “mother and nurse”.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the sisters' lament

traits.title: strict about tears
traits.text: She allowed her nuns “one occasion for tears”: at prayer. When Gregory came to her grieving for Basil, she gave way to his grief “for a little while, like a skilful driver”. Then she reined him in with Paul's words about grieving like those who have no hope.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the sisters' lament; On the Soul and the Resurrection, the opening

traits.title: cheerful to the end
traits.text: Dying of fever, she hid how hard it was to breathe, so as not to upset her brother. “In every way she tried to be cheerful,” Gregory says. She led the talk, and asked questions to keep them talking.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory comes to the monastery

said.lede: Almost everything we know comes from one brother. Gregory of Nyssa wrote her Life soon after she died, from what he saw himself and what those who lived with her told him.

quotes.q: …if indeed she should be styled woman, for I do not know whether it is fitting to designate her by her sex, who so surpassed her sex.
quotes.who: Gregory of Nyssa, at the start of her Life

cite.text: Life of Macrina, introduction

quotes.q: Store-cupboard indeed! You have in front of you all her treasure. There is the cloak, there is the head-covering, there the well-worn shoes on the feet. This is all her wealth, these are her riches.
quotes.who: Lampadia, the deaconess who led the sisters, when Gregory asked for burial clothes

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Vestiana comes to help

quotes.q: Learn what manner of goodness has been taken away from human life.
quotes.who: A soldier from Sebastopolis, a relative, meeting Gregory on the road home from her funeral

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory returns home

moments.title: A secret name
moments.text: Her mother fell asleep in labour and dreamed. Someone “in form and raiment more splendid than a human being” called the baby Thecla, after the famous virgin of St Paul's day. He said it three times, and the birth was easy. Thecla stayed a secret name. To everyone else she was Macrina, after her grandmother.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, her parents and her birth

moments.title: The Psalms, all day
moments.text: Her mother would not teach her the poets, with their tragic passions and crude comedies. She taught her the Bible instead, above all the Wisdom of Solomon. Macrina said the Psalms when she got up and when she went to bed, at her work and at her meals. The Psalter went everywhere with her, “like a good fellow-traveller that never deserted her”.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, her childhood

moments.title: One marriage
moments.text: Her father chose her a husband, a young man of good family who was making his name as a speaker in the law courts. He died before the wedding. Macrina said her father's choice already counted as a marriage, and “there was but one marriage, as there is one birth and one death”. Her fiancé lived to God, she said, and was “absent only, not dead”. She turned down every suitor after him.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, her betrothal and the young man's death

moments.title: Never leaving her mother
moments.text: She resolved never to leave her mother, even for a moment. She cooked her mother's meals herself and helped her run estates spread over three districts. Their mother used to say she carried her other children for a set time, but “Macrina she bore always”. When the youngest, Peter, was born, their father died. Macrina took the baby from his nurse and raised him, and became to him “father, teacher, tutor, mother, giver of all good advice”.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, she resolves never to leave her mother; Peter, the youngest brother

moments.title: Basil comes home
moments.text: Basil came back from his long studies, already a skilled speaker, and full of himself. He “looked down on the local dignitaries”. Macrina took him in hand. He soon gave up his fame and his property for a life of work with his hands.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Basil returns from the university

moments.title: Mistress and maids as sisters
moments.text: She led her mother to give up her grand way of life and share the life of the maids, “treating all her slave girls and menials as if they were sisters”. Mother, daughter and maids ate the same food and slept on the same kind of bed. They prayed and sang hymns day and night, so that “to them this meant work, and work so called was rest”. In a famine, crowds came to them for food, and Peter fed so many that “the desert seemed a city”.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, mother and daughter; Peter, the youngest brother

moments.title: First-fruits and tenth
moments.text: Their mother died with Macrina and Peter sitting on either side of her bed. She laid a hand on each and prayed, “To Thee, O Lord, I give the fruit of my womb as both first-fruits and tenths.” Macrina was her first child, and Peter her tenth. They buried her in their father's grave.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, death of the mother

moments.title: Gregory's last visit
moments.text: Basil died. Nine months or so later, after a synod at Antioch, Gregory set out to see his sister. Exile and church troubles had kept them apart for nearly eight years. He found her lying on a board on the floor, burning with fever. She could not get up, but she raised herself on one elbow to greet him. They talked about Basil, and about the soul and the life to come. Gregory later wrote up their talk as a dialogue.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory resolves to visit his sister; Gregory comes to the monastery

miracles.lede: Gregory tells two healings in full. He names more, and he leaves them out on purpose. Of those, he says:

pledge.q: All are believed to be true, even though apparently incredible, by those who have investigated them accurately.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the conclusion

items.title: The tumour
items.text: A growth appeared on her breast, below the neck, and it threatened to spread to the heart. Her mother begged her to see a doctor. Medicine, she said, was sent by God to save people. Macrina thought uncovering her body for a stranger was worse than the pain. She prayed all night in the sanctuary, weeping, and put the mud from her tears on the sore. Then she asked her mother to make the sign of the cross over it.
items.quote: But when the mother put her hand within her bosom, to make the sign of the cross on the part, the sign worked and the tumour disappeared.
items.witness: Vestiana told Gregory as they laid out her body. She held the lamp close to show him the tiny scar it left.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the story of a scar

items.title: The little girl's eye
items.text: A soldier and his wife came to visit with their small daughter. An illness had left the membrane round her eye swollen and whitish. Macrina held the child, kissed her eyes, and promised them a medicine if they stayed to eat. On the road home they realised they had forgotten it. Then the mother looked at her daughter. The eye was healed.
items.quote: She has indeed given her the true drug which cures disease; it is the healing that comes from prayer.
items.witness: The girl's father told Gregory on his way home from the funeral. He wept as he told it.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the soldier's story

note.text: The father said that on that day he “understood the marvels of the Gospel that hitherto had been incredible” to him.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the soldier's story

more.title: Grain that did not run out
more.text: In a famine, grain was handed out to the hungry again and again, and the heap never got smaller. Gregory heard this from people who lived with her.
more.quote: the corn for the relief of need, though constantly distributed, suffered no perceptible diminution

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the conclusion

more.title: More he left out
more.text: Those who lived with her told him of other wonders. He lists them in one line and leaves it there.
more.quote: Healings of diseases, and castings out of demons, and true predictions of the future.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the conclusion

more.title: Light from her body
more.text: On his way to her, Gregory dreamed three times that he carried martyrs' relics, shining like a mirror turned to the sun. After she died, they laid her mother's dark robe over her. Even so, he says, she seemed to shine, as in his dream.
more.quote: rays actually seemed to shine forth from her beauty

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory's journey and the story of a scar

doubt.title: Gregory expected doubt
doubt.text: He knew some would scoff. What goes beyond a hearer's own experience, he says, “men receive with insult and suspicion of falsehood”. So he left most of the wonders out, “lest the unbeliever should be injured by being led to disbelieve the gifts of God”.

words.note: Macrina wrote nothing that survives. These are her words as her brother Gregory recorded them. The Life, in W. K. Lowther Clarke's translation of 1916, gives what he remembered her saying. His dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection, translated by William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson in 1893, puts his own ideas in her voice.

feature.q: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?
feature.ctx: He had poured out his troubles to her: exile under the emperor Valens, and a Church in turmoil. She told him to compare his life with their parents' lives, and to see where his fame came from.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory returns to Macrina

quotes.q: But you are renowned in cities and peoples and nations. Churches summon you as an ally and director, and do you not see the grace of God in it all? Do you fail to recognise the cause of such great blessings, that it is your parents' prayers that are lifting you up on high, you that have little or no equipment within yourself for such success?
quotes.who: She went on, a moment later.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory returns to Macrina

quotes.q: It is time, brother, for you to rest your body awhile, since it is wearied with the great toil of your journey.
quotes.who: Dying herself, she sent him off to rest.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, she sends Gregory away to rest

quotes.q: Why, what is the especial pain you feel in the mere necessity itself of dying? This common talk of unthinking persons is no sufficient accusation.
quotes.who: In the dialogue, when Gregory said everyone dreads death.

cite.text: On the Soul and the Resurrection, the opening

quotes.q: And who could deny that truth is to be found only in that upon which the seal of Scriptural testimony is set?
quotes.who: In the dialogue, when Gregory asked her to test her reasoning by Scripture.

cite.text: On the Soul and the Resurrection, on the passions

quotes.q: …they are not the soul, but only like warts growing out of the soul's thinking part.
quotes.who: In the dialogue, on anger, desire and the other passions.

cite.text: On the Soul and the Resurrection, on the passions

myths.claim: She suffered in the persecutions and learned from Gregory the Wonderworker.
myths.truth: That was her grandmother, Macrina the Elder. In the Roman Martyrology the grandmother is kept on 14 January, the granddaughter on 19 July.

cite.text: Roman Martyrology (1916), 14 January; Life of Macrina, her parents

myths.claim: Her book, On the Soul and the Resurrection.
myths.truth: She wrote nothing that survives. The dialogue is Gregory's, written in her voice. The New Catholic Encyclopedia says its views are undoubtedly his.

cite.text: New Catholic Encyclopedia; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

myths.claim: She died in her brother's arms.
myths.truth: Gregory does not say so. He says she made the sign of the cross, drew one deep breath and died. Then he laid her hands on her face, as she had asked. It was their mother who died in the arms of her two children, Macrina and Peter.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, her dying prayer and the death of the mother

myths.claim: Her nuns told Gregory how she healed a little girl's eye.
myths.truth: The girl's father told him. He was a soldier from Sebastopolis, and Gregory met him on the road home.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the soldier's story

myths.truth: The Church of England's calendar calls her one. Gregory's Life does not. There the deaconess is Lampadia, “leader of the band of sisters”, and Macrina is the abbess.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Vestiana comes to help; Church of England calendar

stood.lede: Every line comes through her brother Gregory. In the dialogue the ideas are his own, in her voice.
stood.recorder: as her brother Gregory wrote it

deeper.place: on the rich man and Lazarus

all.place: on God being all in all

circle.name: Basil the Great
circle.text: Her younger brother, later the great bishop of Caesarea. He came home from his studies proud of his speaking, and she turned him to a life of poverty and work. In his letters, as the NPNF edition translates them, he never names her.

cite.text: Life of Macrina; Basil, Letters

circle.name: Gregory of Nyssa
circle.text: Her younger brother, bishop of Nyssa. He wrote her Life, and the dialogue that calls her the Teacher. He sat with her as she died. He laid her hands on her face, as she had asked, and helped carry her bier.

cite.text: Life of Macrina; On the Soul and the Resurrection

circle.name: Peter of Sebaste
circle.text: Her youngest brother, born as their father died. She raised him herself. He later led the men's side of the community, and became bishop of Sebaste.

cite.text: Life of Macrina; NPNF volume 8

circle.name: Naucratius
circle.text: The brother next after Basil, and the most gifted. After a speech that thrilled a whole theatre, he left it all to live alone on the Iris. He fished to feed poor old people. Five years later he was brought home dead.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, the story of Naucratius

circle.name: Emmelia
circle.text: Their mother. Macrina never left her side. Emmelia begged her daughter to see a doctor, and in the end lived as an equal with her own maids. She died in the arms of Macrina and Peter.

cite.text: Life of Macrina; Clarke, introduction to the Life

circle.name: Macrina the Elder
circle.text: Their father's mother, who confessed Christ in the persecutions. Macrina was named after her. Basil wrote that he learned about God as a boy from “my blessed mother and my grandmother Macrina”.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, her parents; Basil, Letter 223

circle.name: Lampadia and Vestiana
circle.text: Two of her sisters in the community. Lampadia, a deaconess, led the sisters. Vestiana, a senator's daughter widowed young, had put herself in Macrina's care. They laid out her body with Gregory.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Vestiana comes to help

death.big: She died of a fever in 379 or 380, at her community on the river Iris, with her brother Gregory beside her.
paras: She lay on the floor, on a sack spread over a board. On her last day every breath was hard, but she kept talking to lift her visitors' spirits.

Toward sunset, with her couch turned to the East, she stopped talking to them. She prayed in a low voice that they could only just hear. When the fever dried her tongue, she prayed with her lips and hands. At the lighting of the lamps she tried to join the evening thanksgiving. Then she made the sign of the cross, and she “drew a great deep breath and closed her life and her prayer together”.
Her nuns broke into loud weeping. Gregory reminded them of her rule, and turned their laments into psalms. People streamed in from the whole district for a vigil that lasted all night.

In the morning Gregory and the local bishop, Araxius, took up the front of her bier. The crowds were so thick that the short way to the church of the Holy Martyrs, about a mile, took most of the day. She was laid beside her mother, as both had prayed. Gregory threw himself on the grave and embraced the dust, and then went home.

later.title: Round her neck
later.text: As they dressed her body, Vestiana found an iron cross and an iron ring on a thin thread, resting over her heart. The ring was hollow. Vestiana said it held “a particle of the Cross of Life”. Gregory took the ring, and Vestiana the cross.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, marks of her holiness

items.q: This favour also Thou hast granted me, O God, and hast not deprived me of my desire, because Thou hast stirred up Thy servant to visit Thy handmaid.
items.ctx: When he found her lying on the floor, the day before she died.

items.q: The light of our eyes has gone out, the light that guided our souls has been taken away.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, Gregory comes to the monastery; the sisters' lament

saint.big: Yes. Catholics and Orthodox count her a saint. Anglicans keep her day, and the ELCA remembers her.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England. The Episcopal Church too, 19 July
ELCA, 14 June. Not in the Missouri Synod's calendar

paras: She was honoured soon after she died, and Gregory calls her the saint all through her Life. An unusual number of the Life's manuscripts come from around Pontus, which points to a strong local cult. It spread through the Greek, Egyptian, Syrian and Arab churches. It reached the West late, because the Life was not put into Latin until the 16th century.
She is not on the General Roman Calendar, so most Catholic parishes do not mark her day.

extras.title: Everyone saved in the end?
extras.lede: Gregory's dialogue gives Macrina a bold hope about the end of all things. The views are Gregory's own, in her voice.

items.title: A fire that heals
items.text: Gregory sums up her argument: God's fire is not chiefly punishment. It separates the good in each soul from the evil. She agrees, and adds that the pain will match the amount of evil in each one.
items.quote: That is my meaning; and also that the agony will be measured by the amount of evil there is in each individual.

cite.text: On the Soul and the Resurrection, on the healing fire

items.title: God all in all
items.text: She reads Paul's words that “God will be all in all” to mean that evil itself will be gone. In the end the whole human race shares in God's good things, some made clean in this life and others later.
items.quote: …some having at once in this life been cleansed from evil, others having afterwards in the necessary periods been healed by the Fire.

cite.text: On the Soul and the Resurrection, on God's one end for our race

items.title: What critics said
items.text: Those who hope that all will be saved point to these pages. Later critics said Gregory was following Origen here, but “he was never branded as a heretic”. A later Patriarch of Constantinople, Germanus, claimed that others had slipped the passages in. The English translators reject that. They also warn against claiming Gregory for hope for everyone, since the same dialogue puts a Last Judgment after the resurrection and the cleansing fire.
items.quote: …to claim him as one who favours the doctrine of ‘Eternal Hope’ in a universal sense is hardly possible

cite.text: NPNF volume 5, the preface and the chapter on Gregory's Origenism

extras.title: Her last prayer
extras.lede: She said it on her last evening, facing the East, in a voice so low they could just hear it. Gregory wrote it down, and added, “we need not doubt that it reached God”.

items.text: The whole prayer, as Gregory gives it.
items.quote: Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death. Thou hast made the end of this life the beginning to us of true life. Thou for a season restest our bodies in sleep and awakest them again at the last trump. Thou givest our earth, which Thou hast fashioned with Thy hands, to the earth to keep in safety. One day Thou wilt take again what Thou hast given, transfiguring with immortality and grace our mortal and unsightly remains. Thou hast saved us from the curse and from sin, having become both for our sakes. Thou hast broken the heads of the dragon who had seized us with his jaws, in the yawning gulf of disobedience. Thou hast shown us the way of resurrection, having broken the gates of hell, and brought to nought him who had the power of death—the devil. Thou hast given a sign to those that fear Thee in the symbol of the Holy Cross, to destroy the adversary and save our life. O God eternal, to Whom I have been attached from my mother's womb, Whom my soul has loved with all its strength, to Whom I have dedicated both my flesh and my soul from my youth up until now—do Thou give me an angel of light to conduct me to the place of refreshment, where is the water of rest, in the bosom of the holy Fathers. Thou that didst break the flaming sword and didst restore to Paradise the man that was crucified with Thee and implored Thy mercies, remember me, too, in Thy kingdom; because I, too, was crucified with Thee, having nailed my flesh to the cross for fear of Thee, and of Thy judgments have I been afraid. Let not the terrible chasm separate me from Thy elect. Nor let the Slanderer stand against me in the way; nor let my sin be found before Thy eyes, if in anything I have sinned in word or deed or thought, led astray by the weakness of our nature. O Thou Who hast power on earth to forgive sins, forgive me, that I may be refreshed and may be found before Thee when I put off my body, without defilement on my soul. But may my soul be received into Thy hands spotless and undefiled, as an offering before Thee.

cite.text: Life of Macrina, her dying prayer
